big_idea: Pattern rules also work with numbers up to 1000 — and we now plan, build, translate, table, and lead a parade ourselves.
learning_intention: We are learning to use pattern rules with whole numbers up to 1000, build a number parade, organize it as a table of values, predict a faraway term, and justify the rule formally.
student_learning_goal: I can build a number parade up to 1000, organize it as a table of values, predict term 50, and justify my rule.
success_criteria: I can build a repeating, growing, OR shrinking number parade with whole numbers up to 1000.
I can organize my number parade as a table of values with TERM and VALUE columns.
I can predict term 50 using the rule and justify formally with the sentence frame.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart from previous lessons (PATTERN, OPERATION, +N RULE, ×N RULE, COMPOUND RULE, TABLE OF VALUES, JUSTIFY, GENERALIZE all up — list of class generalizations from L4 should be on chart)
Two pre-built example parades for the opening reveal: (1) growing +75 starting at 75 (75, 150, 225, 300, 375 — terms 1-5), (2) growing ×2 starting at 5 (5, 10, 20, 40, 80 — terms 1-5)
Number line 0-1000 (or thousand chart) visible on the math wall
Hundred chart 0-100 also visible (some children prefer it for smaller-number rules)
Dry-erase markers (one per pair) for writing numbers in laminated parade strips
Calculators (one per pair) — used freely in this lesson
Summative worksheet 'Lead the Number Parade to 1000' (one per child)
Summative rubric (one per child OR one class clipboard with student-name rows pre-filled)
Junior Pattern Conductor certificates printed and ready for the closing ceremony — keep hidden until the ceremony
Optional: small paper crowns or 'Conductor' name tags for the leading phase

minds_on.activity_name: From Animals to Numbers up to 1000
minds_on.hook: All week we have practiced the moves of a Pattern Conductor: identify the operation, name the rule, build the table, predict the faraway term, justify formally. Today YOU put it all together — and Coco's parade goes all the way up to 1000.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Coco. Beside him, lay the +75 example (75, 150, 225, 300, 375).

Say to students: 'All week — repeating, growing, shrinking, operations, multi-step rules, tables of values, far prediction, formal justification. Today the LAST piece: bigger numbers. Up to 1000.'

Point to the +75 parade. 'Read it.' (75, 150, 225, 300, 375.) 'Rule?' (+75.) 'Table relationship?' Some kids will say term × 75. 'Term 10?' (10 × 75 = 750.) 'Term 13?' (13 × 75 = 975.) 'Term 14?' (14 × 75 = 1050 — over 1000!) 'So this rule fits in our number line up to term 13.'

Lay the second example (×2 starting at 5: 5, 10, 20, 40, 80). 'Read.' (5, 10, 20, 40, 80.) 'Rule?' (×2.) 'Term 6?' (160.) 'Term 7?' (320.) 'Term 8?' (640.) 'Term 9?' (1280 — over 1000.) 'So this rule fits up to term 8.'

'Today YOU are the Conductor. Pick a rule — single-step or multi-step. Build the animal parade. Translate to a number parade up to 1000. Organize as a table. Predict term 50. Justify formally. Then LEAD a partner. By end of class, every one of you is a Junior Pattern Conductor — Grade 3 edition.' Tease one certificate.
student_actions: Sit in a circle on the carpet, facing the two example parades.
Read both number parades and predict terms 6, 8, 10 in each.
Confirm at which term each rule crosses 1000 (the ceiling).
Watch the teacher tease the Junior Pattern Conductor certificate.
Repeat the five summative phases aloud: PLAN, BUILD, TRANSLATE, TABLE, LEAD.

action.activity_name: Plan, Build, Translate, Table, Predict-and-Justify, Lead

steps.instruction: Phase 1 — PLAN (5 min). Each child picks a rule (single-step or multi-step), circles the type, writes the rule, and draws their core or first 2 terms. Hand out the summative worksheet. Rule options: repeating (AB/ABB/ABCD), growing (+N or ×N), shrinking (-N), or a multi-step compound rule.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Conductors — first you PLAN. Pick a rule. Write it. Circle the type. Draw your core or first 2 terms. Take 5 minutes.'

steps.instruction: Phase 2 — BUILD an animal parade (6 min). Children draw or sticker their animal parade across an 8-cell strip. For repeating: extend the core. For growing/shrinking: stack more or fewer animals per cell. Loop the FIRST core (repeating) or the JUMP between term 1 and term 2 (growing/shrinking).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now BUILD. Use your rule to fill all 8 cells. Loop the core OR the first jump. Read your parade quietly to check.' Begin one-on-one rubric conferences during this phase.

steps.instruction: Phase 3 — TRANSLATE to a number parade up to 1000 (6 min). Children pick numbers based on their rule type and starting value, then fill the 8-cell number strip. Calculator allowed. Constraint: every value must be ≤ 1000 AND ≥ 0.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now TRANSLATE. Pick numbers between 1 and 1000. Apply your rule for 8 terms. Use a calculator. Use the thousand chart. Make sure every term stays under 1000.' Continue rubric conferences.

steps.instruction: Phase 4 — TABLE (6 min). Children draw a 2-column table of values with TERM (1-8 pre-filled) and VALUE columns and fill in their 8 number-parade values. Headers must say TERM and VALUE.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now the TABLE. Two columns. Headers TERM and VALUE. Eight rows. Copy your number parade into the value column.' Quick-check each table for correct headers.

steps.instruction: Phase 5 — PREDICT AND JUSTIFY term 50 (6 min). Children compute term 50 using the rule shortcut and write a full justification sentence with the frame. If term 50 exceeds 1000 they write OFF THE CHART and find the latest term that fits. This is the deepest C1.3 + C1.4 evidence.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now PREDICT term 50. Use the rule, not drawing. Justify formally with the sentence frame. If term 50 is over 1000, write OFF THE CHART and find the last term that fits.' This is the deepest C1.3 + C1.4 evidence.

steps.instruction: Phase 6 — LEAD, REVISE & REFLECT (11 min). PART A — LEAD (6 min): pairs lead each other through animal-parade → number-parade → table-of-values → term-50 prediction → justification. Partner B names the rule, checks the math, and says one thing they would change. PART B — REVISE & REFLECT (5 min): each child returns to their own worksheet. Find ONE thing to FIX based on partner feedback or self-audit (commonly: off-by-one in the term-50 jumps, table-rule mismatch after term 4, or animal/number parade representing different rules). Pencil the fix. Write ONE sentence explaining WHAT was changed and WHY. Then draw a star next to the proudest part and a question mark next to the trickiest part. The teacher walks the room with the summative rubric clipboard during both halves; the revision sentence is the strongest C1.3 evidence — score it directly.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Two final jobs as Pattern Conductors. First — find a partner. Lead them through your whole worksheet, animals to numbers to table to term-50 to justification. Then trade — they lead you through theirs. Each of you names one thing the other could improve. Then come back to your own desk. Be your own auditor. Find ONE thing on your worksheet that needs fixing. Pencil the fix. Write one sentence explaining WHAT you changed and WHY. Pattern Conductors always check their own work, especially across animals, numbers, tables, and predictions. Then draw a star next to the part you are PROUDEST of and a question mark next to the part that was HARDEST.'

differentiation.for_emerging: Provide a worksheet with the rule type pre-selected (just repeating, e.g., AB) and a small number bank (5, 10, 25, 50). Pre-print the table headers. Predict only term 10, not term 50. Allow a partner to scribe.
differentiation.for_extending: Challenge the child to use a multi-step compound rule from Lesson 2 (e.g., +50 then -10) AND predict term 50. Stretch question during conferences: 'For your rule, write a generalization for ANY term K — using K and your rule.'
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a worksheet with the table pre-drawn and 8 rows pre-numbered. Provide the justification sentence frame pre-printed beside the prediction. Allow a calculator from the start. Use a partner who can scribe. Predict term 20, not term 50.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: After completing the worksheet, the pair stands and PHYSICALIZES the rule. They walk through the first 8 terms, calling out the value at each step. Then they JUMP to term 50 by computing the multiplication shortcut and walking 50 large steps to a designated 'term 50' spot.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: SUMMATIVE evidence. Look at the worksheet artifact and the partner-lead conversation. For each child: did they pick a valid rule, build it correctly, translate to numbers preserving the rule and staying within 0-1000, organize a correct table of values with headers, predict term 50 using the rule (not drawing), and produce a full justification sentence? Score against the 4-level rubric.
formative_check.how_to_record: Score each child on the summative rubric (4 levels × 4 expectations) using the worksheet as primary evidence and the partner-lead conversation as confirming evidence.

consolidation.activity_name: Junior Pattern Conductor Ceremony — Grade 3 Edition
discussion_prompts: Who would like to LEAD the WHOLE class through their parade? (Take 2-3 children.) They read animal, numbers, table, term-50 prediction, and justification while the class chants the rule.
Whose rule produced the BIGGEST term-50 value? Who got closest to 1000 without going over?
What was the trickiest part of the summative? Was it building, translating, tabling, predicting, or justifying?
What is one GENERALIZATION you discovered this week that you will remember for Grade 4?
Coco wants to know — are you a Pattern Conductor now? What does that mean to you?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child receives a Junior Pattern Conductor certificate (the teacher reads it briefly at the front and hands it over with a high five). Each child then leaves the carpet calling out their rule one last time AND the term-50 value as their parade name ('I am Conductor ___, my rule is ___, and at term 50 my parade is ___').

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Completed 'Lead the Number Parade to 1000' summative worksheet plus partner-lead conversation observations. Scored against the 4-level rubric covering all four expectations (C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4). Plus end-of-unit reflection sheet completed alongside the certificate ceremony.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: This is the unit's summative moment. The seven-phase task (Plan-Build-Translate-Table-Predict/Justify-Lead) is designed so the worksheet artifact gives evidence on C1.1 (pattern type and operation), C1.2 (translation across all reps including table), C1.3 (rule + far prediction + formal justification), and C1.4 (numbers up to 1000). The partner-lead conversation upgrades children to Level 4 when they can independently produce the justification sentence AND articulate a generalization.

expanded_walkthrough.title: Phase 5+7 — Predict-Justify and the self-revision audit
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: L5 is the unit's summative — children combine every move from the week into a single performance. Phase 5 (predict and justify term 50) and Phase 7 (revise + reflect) are the two phases that produce the strongest assessment evidence. Phase 5 is where off-by-one errors and rule-misapplication surface; Phase 7 is where children show they can self-audit. The script below covers what to do during these two phases.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Each child has the L5 worksheet on their desk: animal parade strip (8 cells), number parade strip (8 cells), table-of-values frame, term-50 prediction box, justification sentence frame, and revision space. Calculators are out. The summative rubric clipboard has the four expectations (C1.1 - C1.4) as columns, with rows for each child.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
During Phase 5, walk to a child computing term 50 of their +7 rule starting at 3. They might write: 'Term 50 is 50 × 7 + 3 = 353.' Stop. 'Read me your rule and your starting value.' Child: 'Plus 7 starting at 3.' 'And term 1 is...?' Child: '3.' 'And to get from term 1 to term 50, how many jumps?' Watch the answer. If they say 'fifty', that's the off-by-one. Lead them: 'How far from term 1 to term 2?' One jump. 'Term 1 to term 3?' Two jumps. 'Term 1 to term 50?' Forty-nine. 'So term 50 is 3 plus 49 times 7. That's 3 plus 343, which is 346.' Have them rewrite the justification with the corrected jump count.

Move to a child whose multi-step rule is +5 then -2 starting at 10. Term 50 is harder because they need to discover the hidden +3 simple rule, then apply it. 'What does your rule do over a full cycle?' If they say 'goes up by 3', they own it: 'So your hidden simple rule is +3 starting at 10. Term 50 is 10 plus 49 × 3, which is 10 + 147 = 157.' If they don't see it, prompt: 'Apply your rule for two terms. From 10 to what to what?' Walk through 10 → 15 → 13. 'So 10 to 13 in TWO of YOUR steps. That's +3 over 2 steps.' Some children will jump ahead.

During Phase 7 (REVISE & REFLECT): the child reads through all four phases of their worksheet aloud. The teacher's prompt: 'Now play your own auditor. Where might errors hide?' Common find-and-fix moments: (a) the table-of-values lost the rule after term 4 because the child stopped applying it consistently, (b) the term-50 prediction has the off-by-one (50 jumps instead of 49), (c) the animal parade and number parade represent different rules. The child marks the fix in pencil and writes one sentence explaining what they changed and why. THIS sentence is the richest piece of summative evidence — it's metacognition under the rubric. Score it on the C1.3 and C1.4 columns.
expected_student_responses: (Refines fluently) Spots the off-by-one in their own justification, fixes it, writes a clean explanation.
(Refines with prompt) Catches the table-rule mismatch after reading aloud, fixes the table, writes a brief explanation.
(Cannot self-spot) Reads through and says 'looks fine'. Note as L1-L2 on C1.3 (justification).
(Stretched) Writes a justification AND a 'what could have gone wrong' meta-sentence — full self-audit.
common_misconceptions: Term 50 means 50 jumps from term 1. (Off-by-one — it's 49 jumps.)
Compound rules don't have a hidden simple rule. (Child cannot see +5 then -2 is hidden +3.)
Self-revision means erasing and rewriting. (Child treats revision as cosmetic, not conceptual.)
Once justified, a prediction is unconditionally correct. (Child cannot evaluate whether THEIR justification matches THEIR rule, even when they wrote both.)
recovery_moves: Read-aloud audit on every term-K computation. The 'how many jumps from term 1' question forces the off-by-one to surface.
Hidden-simple-rule discovery: 'Apply your rule for one full cycle. What's the net change?' Makes the simpler rule visible.
Pencil-mark protocol for revision: cross out the original, write the fix, write ONE sentence explaining the change. The sentence is the assessment evidence.
Cross-check: have the child read the rule, then read every cell in the parade to verify the rule was applied each time. The mismatch surfaces in 80% of cases.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Summative performance task for the full unit (C1.1, C1.2, C1.3, C1.4). Each child picks a rule, builds an animal parade, translates to a number parade with whole numbers up to 1000, organizes as a table of values, predicts term 50, justifies formally, and leads a partner.

parts_outline.task: Top-of-page header: a 'My Rule' box (3in × 1in, child writes rule label such as AB, +50, -8, ×3, or '+5 then -2'), a 'Pattern Type' box (3in × 0.5in, child circles REPEATING / GROWING / SHRINKING), and a 'My Core or First 2 Terms' workspace (3in × 1.5in). Reference legend: four animals + a small thousand chart in the corner.

An 8-cell parade strip labelled 'My Animal Parade'. Student fills all 8 cells using their rule. Below the strip, a row of 8 boxes labelled 'My Number Parade' for the matching number values (must be 0-1000). Below that, a writing line: 'My starting number: ____'.

An empty 8-row table of values with column headers TERM (1-8 pre-filled) and VALUE (blank). Student fills the value column. Below the table: 'Term 50 = ____. JUSTIFY: I started at ___, the rule is ___, I jumped 49 times to reach term 50, so term 50 = ___.' Bottom: 'My GENERALIZATION: For any term K, the value is ___.'
